 1            Plaintiff Musi Inc. (“Musi”), through its undersigned counsel, hereby brings this civil action
 2   against Defendant Apple Inc. (“Apple”) for breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of
 3   good faith and fair dealing, and alleges as follows:
 4   I.       NATURE OF THE ACTION
 5            1.     This case arises from Apple’s abrupt removal of Musi’s mobile software application
 6   (the “Musi app”) from the Apple App Store (“the App Store”), based upon an unsubstantiated third-
 7   party complaint, and in violation of the parties’ contractual agreements. Despite its obligations to
 8   investigate complaints in good faith, Apple removed the Musi app based upon unsupported
 9   accusations from a third party who has failed to respond to Musi’s communications. Worse, Apple
10   was fully aware that the third party had failed to substantiate its claims to Musi.(the “App Store”), the
11   only commercially viable marketplace for applications for Apple devices. Apple removed the Musi
12   app at the behest of several key players in the music industry, but told Musi it was acting on the basis
13   of a complaint by third-party YouTube (a complaint Apple had purposefully cooked up by proactively
14   seeking to revive a 14-month-old complaint from YouTube that had previously been closed because
15   YouTube had stopped responding). In truth, Apple was acting to appease music-industry players with
16   whom Apple had other commercial dealings. Indeed, Apple later stated that it relied on “evidence”
17   provided by the National Music Publishers Association (“NMPA”)—not by YouTube—that Musi was
18   violating YouTube’s Terms of Service. But Apple knew that this “evidence” was false, as it has since
19   admitted, and it did not disclose this so-called “evidence” to Musi until this litigation. Specifically,
20   Apple’s post hoc justification for removing the Musi app—that Musi was violating YouTube’s Terms
21   of Service with regard to its use of YouTube’s Data/iFrame Application Programming Interface
22   (hereafter, “API”)—was something that Apple knew to be false. Indeed, Apple knew months before
23   the removal—it had learned from the very music-industry players it was acting to appease—that Musi
24   was not using YouTube’s API. Apple’s improper removal of the Musi app has caused—and continues
25   to cause—substantial harm to Musi’s business and reputation.
26            2.     Plaintiff Musi is a mobile computing software company and the developer, owner, and
27   operator of the Musi app, which provides users with enhanced functionality to interact with publicly
28   available content on YouTube’s website through an augmentative interface. Since its inception, and

21   began a backchannel scheme to cook up a supposed reason to remove the Musi app. Specifically, and
22   in an effort to appease its friends in the music industry, Apple proactively reached out to YouTube

20   the Musi app under false pretenses.

22   implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, but also Apple’s own contractual obligations to
23   developers who make applications available on the App Store.

 4   smartphones—branded “iPhones.” iPhones are portable electronic devices that connect wirelessly to
 5   the internet and have advanced computing capabilities, including internet browsing and music
 6   streaming.
 7           14.21. To function, smartphones require a mobile operating system (“mobile OS”). A mobile
 8   OS is piece of software that manages the smartphone’s hardware and allows users to run software
 9   applications developed specifically for use on the smartphone, i.e., “apps.”
10           15.22. iPhones are sold with Apple’s proprietary mobile OS pre-installed, named “iOS.”
11   iPhone users frequently rely on iOS apps developed by Apple, as well as third-party iOS apps, to fully
12   enjoy their iPhone’s capabilities. Apps must be iOS-based to operate on iPhone.
13           16.23. Third-party developers make their iOS apps available to iPhone users primarily through
14   Apple’s App Store. The App Store is an app marketplace developed and operated by Apple for iOS
15   apps. As the developer, owner, and operator of the App Store, Apple contracts with all third-party iOS
16   app developers that distribute their apps using the App Store, including Musi.
17           17.24. The App Store allows iPhone users to browse, search for, and download Apple-
18   developed iOS apps, as well as third-party iOS apps—as long those third-party apps are approved by
19   Apple. Without approval, a third-party iOS app cannot not be made available on the App Store.
20        B. Apple’s Developer Program License Agreement

22   consumers. And as the developer, owner, and operator of the App Store, Apple enjoys singular power
23   to choose which iOS apps are made available. However, these powers are limited by the terms and
24   conditions enumerated in the Developer Agreement. Attached as Exhibit A is a true and correct copy
25   of the Developer Agreement.
26           19.26. Apple drafted the Developer Agreement. The agreement is a contract of adhesion,
27   because Apple requires all third-party iOS developers to enter into the Developer Agreement before
28   they can develop apps using iOS. The Developer Agreement grants third-party developers a limited,

 1                                              DEFINITIONS

 2           1.       “Document(s)” is defined to be synonymous in meaning and equal in scope to the

 3   usage of the term in Rules 26 and 34(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

 4           2.       “Electronically stored information” or “ESI” is to be interpreted broadly, as used

 5   in Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 26 and 34.

 6           3.       “Hard Copy Document(s)” means Documents existing in paper form at the time

 7   of collection.

 8           4.       “Hash Value” is a mathematical algorithm that calculates a unique value for a

 9   given set of data, similar to a digital footprint, representing the binary content of the data to assist

10   in subsequently ensuring that data has not been modified and to facilitate duplicate identification.

11   Unless otherwise specified, hash values shall be calculated using the MD5 hash algorithm.

12           5.       “Load File(s)” are electronic files containing information identifying a set of

13   paper scanned (static) images or processed ESI and indicating where individual pages or files

14   belong together as documents, including attachments, and where each document begins and

15   ends. Load Files also contain data relevant to individual Documents, including extracted and

16   user-created metadata, coded data, as well as OCR or Extracted Text. A load file linking

17   corresponding images is used for productions of static images (e.g., TIFFs).

18           6.       “Metadata” is the term used to describe the application and system information of

19   a file that contains data about the file, as opposed to describing the content of a file, as the term is

20   described and used in the “The Sedona Conference Glossary: E-Discovery and Digital

21   Information Management,” Fifth Ed., February 2020.

22           7.       “Native Format” means and refers to an electronic document’s associated file

23   structure defined by the original creating application and as collected from custodians. For

24   example, the native format of an Excel workbook is an .xls or .xlsx file.

25           8.       “Optical Character Recognition” or “OCR” means the process of recognizing, and

26   creating a file containing, visible text within an image.

 1           Plaintiff Musi Inc. (“Musi”) and Defendant Apple Inc. (“Apple”) hereby agree that the

 2   following procedures shall govern discovery of Electronically-Stored Information (“ESI”) in this

 3   case:

 4           1.     This ESI Stipulation supplements all other discovery rules and orders. It

 5   streamlines ESI production to promote a “just, speedy, and inexpensive determination” of this

 6   action, as required by Rule 1 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

 7           2.     Except as specifically set forth herein, this Order does not alter or affect the

 8   applicability of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (“Federal Rules”) or any Local Rules of this

 9   U.S. District Court (“Local Rules”), as applicable.

10           3.     This ESI Stipulation may be modified for good cause. The parties may agree to

11   modifications, and if so agreed to, shall jointly submit any modifications to the Court. If the

12   parties cannot reach an agreement regarding proposed modifications, the parties shall submit

13   their competing proposals and a summary of their dispute to the Court.

14           4.     The parties reserve their rights under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure,

15   including Rule 26, in connection with this ESI Stipulation and the parties’ respective productions

16   made pursuant thereto.

17           5.     The Parties acknowledge their duty to meet and confer in good faith to try to

18   resolve discovery disputes.

19           6.     By stipulating to this Order and agreeing to produce documents, generally, in a

20   particular form or forms, neither the party producing documents (the “Producing Party”) nor the

21   party receiving documents (the “Receiving Party”) waives any objection to producing any

22   particular document or category of documents on any grounds whatsoever.

23           7.     Nothing in this Order prevents either Party from reviewing documents or

24   information for responsiveness, privilege and confidentiality prior to production.

25           8.     To the extent that a technical term is not defined herein, those technical terms

26   shall be defined by “The Sedona Conference Glossary: E-Discovery and Digital Information

27   Management,” Fifth Ed., February 2020.

28

 1                                              DEFINITIONS

 2           1.       “Document(s)” is defined to be synonymous in meaning and equal in scope to the

 3   usage of the term in Rules 26 and 34(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

 4           2.       “Electronically stored information” or “ESI” is to be interpreted broadly, as used

 5   in Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 26 and 34.

 6           3.       “Hard Copy Document(s)” means Documents existing in paper form at the time

 7   of collection.

 8           4.       “Hash Value” is a mathematical algorithm that calculates a unique value for a

 9   given set of data, similar to a digital footprint, representing the binary content of the data to assist

10   in subsequently ensuring that data has not been modified and to facilitate duplicate identification.

11   Unless otherwise specified, hash values shall be calculated using the MD5 hash algorithm.

12           5.       “Load File(s)” are electronic files containing information identifying a set of

13   paper scanned (static) images or processed ESI and indicating where individual pages or files

14   belong together as documents, including attachments, and where each document begins and

15   ends. Load Files also contain data relevant to individual Documents, including extracted and

16   user-created metadata, coded data, as well as OCR or Extracted Text. A load file linking

17   corresponding images is used for productions of static images (e.g., TIFFs).

18           6.       “Metadata” is the term used to describe the application and system information of

19   a file that contains data about the file, as opposed to describing the content of a file, as the term is

20   described and used in the “The Sedona Conference Glossary: E-Discovery and Digital

21   Information Management,” Fifth Ed., February 2020.

22           7.       “Native Format” means and refers to an electronic document’s associated file

23   structure defined by the original creating application and as collected from custodians. For

24   example, the native format of an Excel workbook is an .xls or .xlsx file.

25           8.       “Optical Character Recognition” or “OCR” means the process of recognizing, and

26   creating a file containing, visible text within an image.

27

28

               Case 5:24-cv-06920-EKL         Document 55         Filed 02/27/25      Page 4 of 12




 1            9.    “Searchable Text” means the native text extracted from ESI and any Optical

 2   Character Recognition text (“OCR text”) generated from a Hard Copy Document or electronic

 3   image.

 4                                           ESI PROVISIONS

 5            1.    Search. The parties agree that in responding to an initial Fed. R. Civ. P. 34
 6   request, or earlier if appropriate, they will meet and confer about methods to search ESI in order
 7   to identify ESI that is subject to production in discovery and filter out ESI that is not subject to
 8   discovery.
 9            2.    Cooperation. The parties are aware of the importance the Court places on
10   cooperation and commit to cooperate in good faith throughout the matter consistent with this
11   Court’s Guidelines for the Discovery of ESI.
12            3.    Format for production of documents – documents existing in electronic
13   format. Except as otherwise provided for in this Stipulation, all documents existing in electronic
14   format shall be produced in either multiple page, searchable PDF format or single-page TIFF
15   format with accompanying extracted text files and .dat and .opt load files for image and metadata
16   loading. The searchable PDF format or single-page TIFF format must be at a resolution of at
17   least 300 dpi in accordance with the following:
18                  A.      PDF or TIFF files shall be produced along with Concordance/Opticon
19   image load files that indicate the beginning and ending of each document, along with additional
20   Metadata fields as described in Exhibit A to this Protocol.
21                  B.      For documents which already exist in PDF format prior to production (i.e.,
22   which the producing party receives from a client or third party in PDF format), the producing
23   party may provide them in that same PDF format, whether searchable or non-searchable. For
24   documents converted to PDF format prior to production, the producing party shall make
25   reasonable efforts to convert to searchable PDF.
26                  C.      Metadata. Load files should include, where applicable, the information
27   listed in the Table of Metadata Fields, attached as Exhibit A. However, the parties are not
28   obligated to include metadata for any document that does not contain such metadata in the

 1   original, if it is not possible to automate the creation of metadata when the document is collected.

 2   The parties reserve their rights to object to any request for the creation of metadata for

 3   documents that do not contain metadata in the original.

 4                  D.      Production media and encryption of productions. Unless otherwise

 5   agreed, the parties shall provide document productions in the following manner: The producing

 6   party shall provide the production data on CDs, DVDs, external hard drives or SFTP, as

 7   appropriate. The producing party shall encrypt the production data using WinRAR encryption,

 8   and the producing party shall forward the password to decrypt the production data separately

 9   from the CD, DVD, external drive or SFTP to which the production data is saved.

10          4.      Format for production of documents – hardcopy or paper documents. All

11   documents that are hardcopy or paper files shall be scanned and produced in the same manner as

12   documents existing in electronic format, including making reasonable efforts to render the

13   documents searchable.

14          5.      Source code. This Stipulation does not govern the format for production of

15   source code.

16          6.      Parent and child emails. The parties shall produce responsive and not privileged

17   email attachments sequentially after the parent email.

18          7.      Native files. The parties will meet and confer to discuss requests for the

19   production of files in native format, on a case-by-case basis. If the parties are unable to reach

20   agreement with regard to requests for additional documents in native-file format, the parties

21   reserve the right to seek relief from the Court. Documents produced natively shall be represented

22   in the set of imaged documents by a slipsheet indicating the production identification number

23   and confidentiality designation for the native file that is being produced.

24          8.      Databases. Certain types of databases are dynamic in nature and will often

25   contain information that is neither relevant nor reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of

26   admissible evidence. The parties agree to meet and confer on acceptable format for production of

27   information from databases and other structured data sources. The parties agree to identify the

 1   specific databases, by name, that contain the relevant and responsive information that parties

 2   produce.

 3           9.      Short Message Discovery. To the extent short messages from mobile devices or

 4   collaboration tools such as Microsoft Teams, Slack, etc. are responsive and not privileged, the

 5   parties agree to meet and confer regarding their production format.

 6           10.     Requests for hi-resolution or color documents. The parties agree to respond to

 7   reasonable and specific requests for the production of higher resolution or color images. Nothing

 8   in this Stipulation shall preclude a producing party from objecting to such requests as

 9   unreasonable in number, timing or scope, provided that a producing party shall not object if the

10   document as originally produced is illegible or difficult to read. The producing party shall have

11   the option of responding by producing a native-file version of the document. If a dispute arises

12   with regard to requests for higher resolution or color images, the parties will meet and confer in

13   good faith to try to resolve it.

14           11.     Foreign language documents. All documents shall be produced in their original

15   language. Where a requested document exists in a foreign language and the producing party also

16   has an English-language version of that document that it prepared for non-litigation purposes

17   prior to filing of the lawsuit, the producing party shall produce both the original document and

18   all English-language versions. In addition, if the producing party has a certified translation of a

19   foreign-language document that is being produced, (whether or not the translation is prepared for

20   purposes of litigation) the producing party shall produce both the original document and the

21   certified translation. Nothing in this agreement shall require a producing party to prepare a

22   translation, certified or otherwise, for foreign language documents that are produced in

23   discovery.

24           12.     Document preservation. The parties have discussed their preservation

25   obligations and needs and agree that preservation of potentially relevant ESI shall be consistent

26   with their obligations set forth in Rule 26 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. The parties

27   represent that they have issued litigation hold notices to individuals whom they reasonably

28   believe to possess relevant documents. To the extent required, the parties represent that they have

Cousins: Motion Hearing held on 2/26/2025 re 46 Motion for Discovery.- Musi's Request for Expedited Discovery, ECF No. 46, is Granted-in-Part and Denied-in-part, as stated on the record. The central issue is whether the discovery sought is targeted, narrow, and proportional to the needs of the case under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26. - The Court determined that witness Elizabeth Miles must be added as a custodian. Responsive non-privileged documents from Miles must be produced by 3/5/2025. - The rest of the discovery is denied.
